claim: Nine inherited neurodegenerative disorders are caused by expansion of a CAG triplet repeat in the protein-coding region of the respective disease genes.
source: Nine inherited neurodegenerative disorders are caused by expansion of a CAG triplet repeat in the protein-coding region of the respective disease genes.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on polyQ diseases

claim: The CAG repeat encodes the amino acid glutamine.
source: The CAG repeat encodes the amino acid glutamine
evidence: Based on established genetic code knowledge

claim: The polyQ family includes six spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 17), Huntington's disease (HD), dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, and Kennedy's disease.
source: The polyQ family includes six spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 17), Huntington's disease (HD), dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, and Kennedy's disease (also known as spinal-bulbar muscular atrophy, or SBMA) (Paulson et al., 1997; Zoghbi and Orr, 2000; La Spada and Taylor, 2003; Todi et al., 2007; Zoghbi and Orr, 2009; Paulson et al., 2017; Lieberman et al., 2019; Buijsen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature

claim: PolyQ pathogenesis involves primarily toxic gain-of-function acquired by the disease protein.
source: Various pathogenic mechanisms are shared, involving primarily toxic gain-of-function acquired by the disease protein.
evidence: Based on established understanding of polyQ disease mechanisms

claim: PolyQ mutations yield aggregation of the toxic polyQ protein.
source: These mutations yield aggregation of the toxic polyQ protein
evidence: Based on established knowledge of polyQ protein behavior

claim: Despite wide expression of polyQ proteins throughout the body, only select central nervous system regions degenerate in each disease.
source: despite their wide expression throughout the body, only select central nervous system regions degenerate in each disease.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of polyQ disease pathology

claim: Common mechanisms underlying polyQ pathogenesis include mitochondrial, transcriptional, and autophagic dysfunction.

claim: The individual host proteins in polyQ diseases have divergent functions.
source: Although the disorders share disease mechanisms, the individual host proteins have divergent functions (Zoghbi and Orr, 2000; La Spada and Taylor, 2003; Todi et al., 2007; Zoghbi and Orr, 2009; Paulson et al., 2017; Lieberman et al., 2019; Buijsen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature

claim: There is currently no therapeutic solution for any polyQ disease.

claim: Endurance exercise is a low-cost, effective intervention with broad pro-healthspan effects.
source: Endurance exercise is a low-cost, effective intervention with broad pro-healthspan effects, including reducing the incidence of obesity, heart disease, cancer, and cognitive defects (Booth et al., 2012; Wilmot et al., 2012; Strasser, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature

claim: In the context of neurodegenerative disease, Sesn may protect mobility until oxidative burden in neurons becomes insurmountable.
source: Perhaps, in the context of neurodegenerative disease, Sesn protects mobility until oxidative burden in neurons becomes insurmountable.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental results

claim: Wild-type Sesn overexpression in SCA2 model flies correlated with significantly reduced disease protein and increased autophagic flux.
source: Wild-type Sesn overexpression in SCA2 model flies correlated with significantly reduced disease protein and increased autophagic flux.
evidence: Based on Western blot data for ATXN2 and autophagy markers

claim: Overexpression of mutated versions of Sesn also led to reduced disease protein levels.
source: Overexpression of mutated versions of Sesn also led to reduced disease protein levels.
evidence: Based on Western blot data

claim: Some protective mechanisms may directly depend on reduced toxic protein levels.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest the possibility of separate mechanisms at play: some protective mechanisms may directly depend on reduced toxic protein levels (as observed before in a model of HD and exercise Mangiarini et al., 1996; van Dellen et al., 2008)
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to HD studies

claim: Some protective mechanisms may protect independently of changes in degenerative protein levels.
source: others may protect independently of changes in degenerative protein levels, or perhaps without directly relying on it.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental results

claim: Endurance exercise is a promising therapeutic intervention for polyQ neurodegeneration, particularly in SCA2.
source: To conclude, we propose endurance exercise as a promising therapeutic intervention for polyQ neurodegeneration, particularly in SCA2.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from the study

claim: Sesn can substitute for exercise benefits in flies that do not exercise.
source: We also demonstrate that Sesn can substitute for exercise benefits in flies that do not exercise.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing Sesn overexpression improves phenotypes without exercise

claim: Many patients with polyQ diseases will eventually lose the ability to exercise.
source: Identification of molecular targets capable of inducing exercise-like enhancements in the presence of neurodegeneration is particularly important, as many patients will eventually lose the ability to exercise.
evidence: Based on knowledge of disease progression

claim: Expression of polyQ disease proteins in flies causes reduced motility and neuronal cell death.
source: Expression of polyQ disease proteins in flies causes reduced motility and neuronal cell death, as we and others have shown in various publications (Bonini and Fortini, 2003; Perrimon et al., 2016; Pandey and Rajamma, 2018; Ueyama and Nagai, 2018; Tsou et al., 2015a; Sutton et al., 2017; Ristic et al., 2018; Jackson et al., 1998; Fernandez-Funez et al., 2000; Romero et al., 2008; Hsu et al., 2014; Rosas-Arellano et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Full-length, human disease protein was expressed through the binary, RU486-inducible Gal4-UAS system in all fly neurons and only during adulthood, which is toxic.
source: Full-length, human disease protein was expressed through the binary, RU486-inducible Gal4-UAS system (Sujkowski et al., 2015; Brand et al., 1994) in all fly neurons and only during adulthood, which is toxic (Tsou et al., 2013; Tsou et al., 2015a; Tsou et al., 2015b; Costa et al., 2016; Tsou et al., 2016; Sutton et al., 2017; Ristic et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to methodology and toxicity studies

claim: The exercise protocol drives reproducible effects that are robust across genotypes.
source: We have established an optimized exercise protocol (Figure 1B) that drives reproducible effects that are robust across genotypes (Piazza et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The effects of the exercise protocol are not due to non-specific stress or behavioral effect of the regimen.
source: These effects are not due to non-specific stress or behavioral effect of the regimen—unexercised flies exposed to training, but prevented from running, do not experience improvements (Piazza et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to control experiments

claim: Exercised wild-type flies retained faster climbing speed than age-matched, unexercised siblings.
source: Exercised wild-type flies retained faster climbing speed than age-matched, unexercised siblings (Sujkowski and Wessells, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study
